hokusai_c: a woodblock printshop and handscroll hall: Thirty Six Views of New York. Real hook: the Met has shown Hokusai prints; Japan Society on East 47th Street. Trick: a long scroll gallery that unrolls as you walk, and from one marked spot the Empire State Building sits in every piece like Fuji.

My draft for the C rooms in this batch:
lichtenstein_c: his Interiors (1990s paintings of rooms with art on the walls) and the 1993 Guggenheim retrospective. The hall is a Lichtenstein Interior you walk inside: every surface drawn in black outline, flat primary colour and Ben-Day dots, a sofa, a lamp, a plant, all flat, and MLow's pieces hang in it as the only fully detailed things. Trick: toon outline plus halftone shading on the architecture only, so the art pops; walk to the exact spot and the whole hall lines up into one framed comic panel.
dali_c: the Julien Levy Gallery, Madison Avenue, 1933, where The Persistence of Memory was first shown in America (1932 Surrealism show?) or MoMA's 1941 Dali retrospective. Trick: the frames and the pieces melt and drip down the wall while you stare at them, and set back when you look away; the floor is a long sloping perspective that is shorter than it looks.
warhol_c: Leo Castelli, April 1966, Cow Wallpaper and Silver Clouds, the show where he said he was retiring from painting. Pieces hang on cow wallpaper (we can use our own repeating eye flower cow), silver pillows float and drift when you walk into them. Trick: every piece hangs as a silkscreen grid that repeats it four or nine times in shifting inks as you walk past; the clouds bump and reflect the art.

vangogh_c: MoMA, November 1935, Vincent van Gogh, the first blockbuster (huge crowds), or the Bedroom painting with its skewed walls. Trick: the hall is an Ames room built on the Bedroom's perspective, so walking from one corner to the other you grow and shrink against the pieces; or the brush strokes flow out of the frames over the walls as you walk.
picasso_c: MoMA, November 1939, Picasso: Forty Years of His Art, the show that brought Guernica to New York; or the 1980 MoMA retrospective that took the whole museum. Trick: a faceted cubist hall where each piece hangs on hinged panels that show it from three angles at once, and the hall folds as you move.
banksy_c: Housing Works thrift shop, Eighth Avenue, October 2013, where he donated a thrift store landscape he had painted a Nazi officer into, The Banality of the Banality of Evil, later sold at auction for 615,000 dollars. The hall is the thrift shop: MLow's pieces hang in mismatched secondhand frames with handwritten price tags among lamps and racks. Trick: price tags change when you are not looking; one painting in the shop has a stencil figure added only when seen through your phone (a screen in the room).
